approachQuestion.prompt:
Two cargo pieces

Given integer weights and a target T, return whether two DISTINCT array positions have weights summing to T. Repeated weights are allowed. The array may be reordered; return only a Boolean.

Constraints: 2 ≤ n ≤ 200,000; 0 ≤ weights[i] ≤ 1,000,000,000; 0 ≤ T ≤ 2,000,000,000. Exact constant-time arithmetic is available. Compare-based methods only; hashing, radix, counting and bucket structures are outside this task model.

Examples: weights=[4,9,4], T=8 → true. weights=[4,9], T=8 → false. weights=[1,5,12], T=10 → false.

Choose the most efficient valid method among these options under the stated model; avoid removable repeated work.
constraints: The complete input/output and mutation contract in the prompt applies to every option.

options.text: Sort the weights; start at opposite ends. While the indices differ, return true on equality, move the left index inward if the sum is too small, otherwise move the right inward. Return false if they meet.
options.feedback: A too-small sum rules out the current smallest value with every remaining partner; the symmetric rule eliminates the largest value when the sum is too large. Distinct indices prevent reusing one piece.

options.text: Sort weights and check only adjacent pairs for the target sum.
options.feedback: A valid pair need not be adjacent: [1,4,8] with T=9 needs 1 and 8.

options.text: For each weight, binary-search the sorted array for its complement, allowing the search to return the same position.
options.feedback: This can reuse a piece: [4,9] with T=8 finds the same 4 twice and incorrectly returns true.

options.text: Compare every pair of distinct positions and return true if any pair meets the target.
options.feedback: This is correct across the domain, but repeated pair comparisons are avoidable after ordering the values.

feedback.reason: After sorting, a too-small sum permits discarding only the smaller endpoint, while a too-large sum permits discarding only the larger.
details: Comparison merge sort the array, then execute the opposite-end scan with left strictly less than right and the stated sum-directed movements.

complexityQuestion.prompt: Analyze only the revealed method using conventional comparison merge sort with a linear merge buffer and a logarithmic recursion stack. Choose the tightest worst-case time and auxiliary-space bounds in n. Count all working copies, indexed records, buffers and stack frames; exclude the caller input and returned output. No hashing is used. Comparisons, arithmetic, record copies and array accesses take constant time; preallocate output capacity so no resizing assumption is needed.

options.text: O(n log n) time, O(n) additional space
O(n log n) time, O(1) additional space

feedback.reason: Sorting dominates the subsequent linear opposite-end scan.
details: Sorting dominates the linear scan: O(n log n) worst-case time. The merge buffer use O(n) auxiliary memory; the O(log n) recursion stack does not change this total. The output is excluded. The quadratic-time option overstates the tight bound, constant space omits the buffer, and linear time omits comparison sorting.
